content.text:
Я выбрал кандидата 7. Все цифры я считал приблизительно в уме, полного посуточного расчёта не делал, поэтому это оценка, а не точный ответ.

1. **Заказ через день экономит фиксированный платёж.** При ежедневных заказах платёж 19 за день набегает примерно на 28 дней. Заказ через день убирает около 15 таких платежей, это примерно 285. Из планов с заказом через день (6 и 7) у кандидата 7 есть надбавка 1,08× сверх прогноза, а у кандидата 6 нет.
2. **Небольшой перезаказ почти ничего не стоит.** Партия годна 9 дней, поэтому лишние единицы обычно продаются в следующие дни, а не списываются. Хранение дешёвое: 0,4 и 0,2 за единицу в день. Нехватка обходится дорого: теряется маржа 5 и платится неустойка 5 за товар 0 или 8 за товар 1. Средний множитель спроса около 1,046, так что план ровно по прогнозу будет систематически недобирать.
3. **Всплеск спроса покрыт.** Заказ дня 22 товара 0 (130 ед.) приходит в день 24, когда прогноз 78. Заказ дня 22 товара 1 (150 ед.) приходит в день 25, когда прогноз 123. В эти дни не приходит ничего другого, и при вместимости 268 переполнения, похоже, нет.
4. **Конец месяца урезан разумно.** Последний заказ дня 26 (70 и 25) почти совпадает с прогнозом на последние дни, так что непроданного остатка, который в конце ничего не стоит, остаётся мало.

Ежедневные планы (0, 2, 3, 4, 5) теряют на фиксированных платежах. Кандидат 1 заказывает раз в три дня, но его крупные партии упираются во вместимость склада и дают больше хранения.

I estimated this roughly in my head, so the pick isn't certain. **Candidate 3** looks best, ahead of 4 and 7.

1. **Leftover stock carries over.** Goods last 9 days and the oldest batches sell first, so extra stock is usually sold later and only costs holding (0.2–0.4 per unit per day). A missed sale costs the lost margin of 5 plus a penalty of 5–8. A buffer of about 5–10% above the forecast is therefore worth it, especially since actual demand averages about 4.6% above forecast.
2. **Candidate 3 has a buffer of about 8%.** Candidates 0 and 2 order exactly at forecast for at least one product, so they run short more often. Candidate 5 orders about 15% above forecast for most of the month, which builds costly excess stock, then cuts back too far just before the day-25 demand spike.
3. **Ordering less often doesn't pay off here.** Ordering every 2 days (candidates 6 and 7) or every 3 days (candidate 1) saves about 250–340 in the 19-per-day order fee. That is roughly cancelled or exceeded by holding the larger stock between deliveries: about 300 extra for every 2 days and about 600 for every 3 days.
4. **Candidate 3 vs. 4.** Both order daily with a buffer. Candidate 3's buffer is slightly larger (about 8% vs. 5%), and it orders less near the end, when stock left after day 29 is worth nothing.

**Ответ: кандидат 3.** Это оценка в уме, без точной симуляции; разница между кандидатами 3 и 4 небольшая.

1. **Частота заказов.** Кандидаты 6 и 7 заказывают через день и экономят около 266 на сборах по 19. Зато каждые два дня они держат на складе лишний дневной запас, и хранение обходится примерно в 300. Кроме того, в день 22 они заказывают только 150 единиц товара 1 на пик дней 25–26, где спрос около 175. Дефицит выйдет 25+ единиц по 13 упущенной прибыли и неустойки. Кандидат 1 заказывает раз в три дня. У него хранение ещё дороже и есть риск переполнить склад на 268 единиц.
2. **Запас прочности.** Нехватка стоит дорого: 10 за единицу товара 0 и 13 за единицу товара 1. Лишняя единица стоит дёшево: хранение 0,2–0,4 в день, годность 9 дней. Поэтому выгодно заказывать заметно больше прогноза, тем более что средний множитель спроса ≈ 1,046. Кандидат 0 заказывает ровно по прогнозу и потому будет систематически недопоставлять. У кандидата 2 товар 0 тоже ровно по прогнозу.
3. **Кандидаты 3, 4 и 5.**
   - Кандидат 4 заказывает около 1,06 от прогноза, то есть почти без запаса сверх среднего спроса.
   - Кандидат 3 заказывает 1,07–1,09 от прогноза, а в последние дни снижает заказы. Так он расходует накопленный запас и не покупает то, что останется в конце и ничего не будет стоить.
   - Кандидат 5 заказывает около 1,15 от прогноза. Запас у него будет примерно по 80 единиц каждого товара, хранение дороже. Около дня 25 вместе с крупными поставками (90 и 141) склад, вероятно, превысит 268, и излишек пропадёт.

Кандидат 3 даёт лучший баланс между дефицитом, хранением и остатками в конце.

I picked **candidate 7**. I worked this out in my head without a simulation, and candidate 3 is a close second.

1. **Order fees, and why candidate 1 is out.** Plans that order every day (0, 2, 3, 4, 5) pay the 19 fee about 28 times, roughly 532. Ordering every two days (6, 7) cuts that to 14 times, about 266. Ordering every three days (1) saves about 76 more, but stock then sits on the shelf a full extra day. That adds about 0.4·35 + 0.2·35 ≈ 21 a day, or around 600 in holding over the month, which is far more than the saving. It also risks overflowing the 268-unit warehouse around the demand spikes on days 24–25.

2. **Two-day plans against daily plans.** Batching every two days adds about half a day of stock on average, roughly 11 a day or about 330 in holding over the month. That nearly cancels the 266 saved in fees. The tie-breaker is the risk of running out. A daily plan can run short on any day. A two-day batch can only run short on the second day of each cycle, because the morning delivery covers both days. With 30 % noise and a random-walk buffer, a stockout costs 10–13 per unit (lost margin plus penalty). Halving the number of risky days should save several hundred, more than the roughly 60 net difference above.

3. **Same total supply.** Candidate 7 and the best daily plan, candidate 3, deliver almost the same amount of product 0 for days 2–23 (825 vs 824). Both are about 8 % above forecast, which is right because real demand averages about 4.6 % above forecast. Both also run their stock down near the end, so little is wasted on day 29.

4. **Candidate 6 vs candidate 7.** Candidate 6 orders exactly the forecast after a starting buffer of 40. Since true demand runs about 4.6 % above forecast, it falls behind over time. Candidate 7 keeps a margin of about 8 %, and stockouts cost more than the extra holding.

The early shortages on days 0–2 can't be avoided by any plan, so they don't change the ranking.

**Выбор: кандидат 7.** Я сравнивал прикидками в уме, ничего не моделировал. Точный итог ни одного плана я не считал, а заявленным авторами цифрам не доверял.

1. **Фиксированные платежи.** Ежедневный заказ (кандидаты 0, 2–5) стоит около 28 × 19 ≈ 530. Заказ через день (кандидаты 6 и 7) — около 14 × 19 ≈ 270. Поэтому планы через день сразу выигрывают примерно 260.
2. **Нехватка обходится дороже излишка.** Недопроданная единица теряет маржу 5 и вдобавок неустойку 5 (товар 0) или 8 (товар 1). Хранение лишней единицы стоит лишь 0,2–0,4 в день, а при годности 9 дней списаний почти нет. Средний множитель спроса 1,046, поэтому заказ с надбавкой 1,08× и страховым запасом лучше, чем ровно по прогнозу. По этой причине кандидат 7 сильнее кандидата 6, у которого надбавки нет.
3. **Сроки поставки совпадают.** Заказ товара 0 приходит на 2-й день, товара 1 — на 3-й, и каждая партия кандидата 7 покрывает ровно два следующих дня спроса. Например, заказ дня 0 (89 ед. товара 0) приходит в день 2 и покрывает спрос дней 2–3 (59) × 1,08 плюс запас около 25. Склад на 268 единиц при этом не переполняется.
4. **Почему не кандидат 1 (раз в три дня).** Он экономит лишь около 76 на фиксированных платежах. Взамен он платит больше за хранение (примерно 300 за месяц) и заказывает всего около 1,05× без переходящего запаса, так что нехватки при колебаниях спроса будут чаще.

Слабое место кандидата 7 — всплеск спроса на товар 1 в день 25: заказ дня 22 даёт 150 при ожидаемом спросе около 175 за дни 25–26. У кандидата 6 там тоже 150, а по остальным признакам 7 лучше.

I estimated this by hand, as the task required: no code was run. I chose **candidate 5** because it should have the highest expected profit.

1. **Ordering every day is slightly better than ordering in batches.** Candidates 1, 6 and 7 save 19 on each day they skip, but they pay more to store the extra stock between deliveries. For a 3-day cycle (candidate 1), storage costs about 63 per cycle and the skipped fees save 38, so it loses roughly 250 over the month. For a 2-day cycle (6, 7), storage of about 21 per cycle roughly cancels the 19 saved, so there's no real gain.

2. **Candidates 0 and 2 order too little or too much.** Candidate 0 orders exactly the forecast, but real demand averages about 4.6% above the forecast. Its stock slowly runs short, and every missing unit costs a penalty (5 for product 0, 8 for product 1). Candidate 2 orders about 15% extra of product 1 for the whole month, so surplus builds up and is left over at the end.

3. **Candidates 3, 4 and 5 order similar totals, but at different times.**
   - Product 0: candidate 5 orders 1071 in total, candidate 4 orders 1069 and candidate 3 orders 1073. Expected demand for the days these orders can cover (days 2–29) is about 1050.
   - Product 1: candidate 5 orders 1169 and candidate 4 orders 1152. Expected demand for days 3–29 is about 1133. Ordering a little extra makes sense here because a shortage costs 13 per unit (lost margin plus penalty) and storage costs only 0.2 per day.

4. **Candidate 5 has the best timing.** It orders about 15% above forecast in the middle of the month, which builds a buffer against random demand when shortage penalties matter. It then cuts orders on days 23–27, so little stock is left at day 29, when leftovers are worth nothing. Candidate 4 does the opposite: it orders more at the end (47 and 41 on days 26–27), which adds leftover stock. Candidate 3 sits between the two.

All plans run short on days 1–2, because the starting stock can't cover them and orders take 2–3 days to arrive. That doesn't change the comparison.

I picked **candidate 7**, estimated in my head as you asked; nothing was simulated, so this is a judgement call.

1. **Ordering cost vs. storage cost.** Every day with an order costs 19. The daily plans (0, 2, 3, 4, 5) order on about 28 days, which is roughly 532. Ordering every 2 days (plans 6 and 7) means about 15 order days, roughly 285. Ordering every 3 days (plan 1) means about 11 order days, roughly 209. On the other side, bigger and rarer deliveries leave more stock on the shelf. Every extra half-day of demand kept in stock costs about 0.5 × (0.4·35 + 0.2·35) ≈ 10.5 per day, or about 150 over the month.
   - Going from 2-day to 3-day ordering saves about 76 in order fees but adds about 150 in storage, so it doesn't pay.
   - Going from daily to 2-day ordering saves about 247 in order fees but adds only about 150 in storage, so it does pay.

   That makes a 2-day cycle the best of the three.

2. **Order volume vs. expected demand.** Shortages are expensive: lost margin plus penalty is about 10 per unit for product 0 and 13 for product 1. Leftover stock just carries over and costs little to store, so it's better to order a bit too much than too little. Expected demand is the forecast × 1.046.
   - Expected demand that the orders need to cover is about 1050 units of product 0 and about 1134 of product 1.
   - Plan 7 orders 1080 and 1146, which is slightly above expected demand.
   - Plan 6 orders 1030 and 1108, which is below it and risks costly shortages.

   Larger deliveries every 2 days also absorb random swings in demand better than daily orders do.

I pick **candidate 5**, but the margin over candidates 3 and 7 isn't certain. I worked this out in my head without simulating it.

**Why candidate 5 looks best**
- **Running short costs more than ordering too much.** A missing unit costs about 10 for product 0 and 13 for product 1: lost profit of 5 plus the penalty. Extra stock only costs 0.2–0.4 per day to hold, because units keep for 9 days and the oldest sell first. In the worst case, unsold stock at the end loses its purchase price of 7.
- **The plans don't react to actual demand.** Missed sales are lost, so a plan that orders exactly the forecast runs short often. Actual demand also averages about 1.046 times the forecast, not 1.0.
- **Candidate 5 orders the most and plans the ending best.** It orders about 1.15 times the forecast on most days. Over days 23–27 it cuts orders below forecast (about 78 fewer units of product 0 and about 52 fewer of product 1). That uses up the extra stock built earlier, so less is left unsold at day 29.

**How the others compare**
- **Candidate 0** orders exactly the forecast, and candidate 2 does the same for product 0. Both will run short often.
- **Candidates 3 and 4** order about 1.08 and 1.05 times the forecast, so they have smaller buffers. Candidate 3 trims its ending orders slightly; candidate 4 orders a bit more at the end.
- **Candidates 6 and 7** order every other day, which saves about 266 in order fees. Carrying stock overnight costs about the same, so they come out roughly even on that. Their buffer is smaller: about 1.0 times the forecast for candidate 6 and 1.08 for candidate 7.
- **Candidate 1** orders every third day, which saves the most in fees. But its stock comes close to the 268-unit limit, especially when about 296 units ordered on day 22 arrive on days 24–25.

**Main risk for candidate 5:** on day 25 its stock could go over the 268-unit limit, and roughly 40–50 units of product 1 could be lost. Most of those would have been spare stock anyway, so I don't think it changes the ranking.

I estimated this in my head without running anything, and I picked **candidate 7**.

1. **Ordering every other day is about right.** Each day you order costs 19, so ordering every second day saves about 14 × 19 ≈ 266 compared with ordering daily (candidates 0, 2, 3, 4, 5). The extra storage cost is small. That's because storage is cheap (0.4 and 0.2 per unit per day) and two days' stock stays well under the 268-unit limit.
2. **Ordering every three days (candidate 1) costs more than it saves.** It drops about four more order days, saving about 76. But it holds roughly half a day more stock all month, which costs about 10 per day × 30 ≈ 300 in storage.
3. **Candidate 7 beats candidate 6 because it orders more.** A missed sale costs 10 (5 lost margin plus a 5 penalty) for product 0 and 13 (5 + 8) for product 1. A unit left over costs at most 7 if it expires, plus a little storage. Average demand also runs about 4.6% above forecast. Candidate 7 orders 1.08× forecast, while candidate 6 orders exactly the forecast. Candidate 7 also brings 130 units of product 0 for the day-24 spike, against 120.
4. **Candidate 7's timing works.** Product 0 arrives on even days and product 1 on odd days, so the two products never compete for space on the same morning. Both candidates 6 and 7 bring 150 of product 1 for the day-25 spike, so they are even there. Candidate 7's last orders end the month with little stock that would go unsold.

I'd pick **candidate 5**, but only narrowly over candidates 3 and 7. All of this is mental arithmetic on the forecast values; I didn't simulate anything.

1. **What a shortage costs compared with extra stock.** A missing unit of product 0 costs 10 (5 lost margin plus the 5 penalty). For product 1 it costs 13. Keeping a spare unit costs only 0.4 or 0.2 per day. Unsold stock carries over (nothing ships after 9 days), so a safety buffer pays off. The one real risk is stock left on day 29, which is a wasted 7 per unit.
2. **Losses all plans share.** Every plan runs short at the start, because the first orders don't arrive until day 2 or 3. That's about 27 units of product 0 and about 35 of product 1.
3. **Daily plans (0, 2, 3, 4, 5).** Plan 0 orders exactly the forecast. Actual demand averages about 4.6% above forecast, so its stock drifts down and shortages keep repeating. Plan 4 orders about 1.05× the forecast, which builds almost no buffer. Plan 2 only adds buffer to product 1. Plan 3 orders about 1.1× and adds about 27 units up front, but at the end it barely reduces orders, so roughly 50 units of each product are probably left over. Plan 5 orders about 1.15×, so its buffer grows by about 4 units a day. That matches how the spread of cumulative demand grows. It also cuts orders sharply in the last days (product 0 draws down about 58 units, product 1 about 52), so less is left at the end.
4. **Batch plans (1, 6, 7).** Ordering every 2 days saves about 13 × 19 ≈ 250 in daily order fees. Holding two days' stock at a time costs about 11 per day, around 280 over the month. The two roughly cancel out. Plan 6 orders exactly the forecast, so it falls short more often. Plan 7 orders about 1.08× and also reduces orders at the end, which puts it close to plans 3 and 5. Plan 1 orders every 3 days at only about 1.05× the forecast, so it carries more stock without adding safety.
5. **When demand varies.** Shortages become more likely later in the month, so a buffer that keeps growing (plan 5) protects better than a fixed one added up front (plans 3 and 7). Plan 5's large end-of-month cut also lowers the risk of unsold stock on day 29.

Plans 3 and 7 are close enough that a full simulation could put either one ahead.

I picked **candidate 1**. I worked this out in my head without running a simulation, so it's a judgement call, not an exact calculation.

- **Fewer order days:** each day you order anything costs a flat 19. Candidate 1 orders on 10 days (about 190 in fees). Candidates 6 and 7 order every other day (about 250). Candidates 0 and 2–5 order nearly every day (about 530). The other costs don't differ enough to make up that gap.
- **Order sizes fit the forecast:** each batch covers about three days of forecast demand plus roughly 20% extra. That's a sensible buffer against random demand, and it doesn't waste goods because each batch can be sold for 9 days.
- **Fits the warehouse:** product 1 arrives a day after product 0, so stock should stay below the 268-unit limit. That includes the spike on days 24–25, when the 170 units of product 1 arrive with about 230 units in stock in total.
- **Little left over at the end:** the last orders roughly match forecast demand for days 26–29, so not much is left in stock after day 29.
- **Candidates 6 and 7:** their first orders are much larger than the forecast for the days they cover. On top of that, they pay more in order fees than candidate 1.

The biggest risk with candidate 1 is shortages when real demand comes in well above the forecast late in a three-day cycle. I still think the fee savings outweigh that.

I pick **Candidate 3**. Candidate 7 is a close second. I did all of this by hand, so the margins are approximate.

**Where every plan starts the same.** No order arrives before day 2 (product 0) or day 3 (product 1). So every plan runs short at the start, by about 27 units of product 0 and 35 of product 1. Unmet demand is lost, not carried forward, so this loss is the same for all plans and doesn't count against any of them later.

**What separates the plans**

- **Safety stock.** Real demand runs about 4.6% above the forecast on average. Leftover stock carries forward and lasts 9 days, so extra stock costs only 0.2–0.4 per unit per day to keep. A missed sale costs 10 (product 0) or 13 (product 1): the lost margin plus the penalty. Because shortfalls are lost and surpluses carry over, the gap between stock and demand drifts randomly, by about ±50 units by day 25. A real buffer pays for itself.
  - Candidates 0 and 2 order roughly the forecast. Their buffer is gone by mid-month, so they keep running short.
  - Candidates 4 and 6 add about 5% or nothing beyond a first-order cushion. Their buffer ends near zero, about 0–25 units.
  - Candidate 1 orders every 3 days with only about 5% extra. Its buffer stays near zero, and every 3-day cycle adds holding cost.
- **Order fees and holding.** Ordering every 2 days (Candidates 6 and 7) saves about 266 in daily fees. But stock sits longer between deliveries, which adds about 290 in holding costs, so it roughly breaks even. Ordering every 3 days (Candidate 1) saves about 320 in fees but adds about 570 in holding.
- **Storage limit on day 25.** Product 1 demand spikes to 123 that day, and the warehouse holds 268 units. Product 0 is accepted first, so overflow comes out of product 1.
  - Candidate 5 starts with almost no buffer, then builds one too big. On day 25 it overflows by about 50 units.
  - Candidate 7 overflows by about 30 units. Its product 1 delivery for days 25–26 is also already about 25 units short, so it risks running short of product 1, which carries the higher penalty.
  - Candidate 3 overflows by only about 10–15 units.

**Why Candidate 3**
- It orders a solid cushion on day 0 (+27 per product).
- After that it orders about 10% above forecast. That outpaces the 4.6% upward drift, so it holds a buffer of about 50–60 units without big overflow.
- It cuts orders in the last days so little stock is left unsold at the end.

Candidate 7 has a similar buffer, but its fee savings are cancelled by extra holding costs, and it does worse on day 25.

I picked candidate 5. I compared the plans by rough mental estimates, not a full simulation, so this is a judgement call rather than a proven optimum.

- **How often to order:** Ordering every day costs about 19 per day in fees. Ordering every 2–3 days saves fees but means holding more stock, which costs about as much. So the order rhythm doesn't separate the plans much.
- **Ordering above forecast:** Running out costs much more than holding stock. A missing unit loses the 5 margin plus a penalty of 5 (product 0) or 8 (product 1). A unit held one more day costs only 0.4 or 0.2. Actual demand also averages about 4.6% above forecast. So a plan should order above forecast to build a safety buffer.
  - Candidates 0 and 2 order exactly the forecast for at least one product, so any starting buffer wears away and shortages follow.
  - Candidates 3 and 4 do order above forecast, but they don't cut back near the end. Several dozen units of each product would be left over, and each cost 7.
- **Candidate 5:** It orders about 15% above forecast, which builds a good buffer. On days 23–27 it orders below forecast so the buffer gets sold off, leaving little unsold stock at the end. It also orders 141 of product 1 on day 22, which arrives on day 25, the demand spike day (forecast 123).
- **Main risk:** Its first order is small (30 of product 0), so it may run short on days 2–3.
- **Runner-up:** Candidate 7 orders every 2 days at about 8% above forecast and also cuts back at the end. It's close, but by my estimate slightly behind.

Я выбрал кандидата 3. Это оценка в уме, а не точная симуляция. Вывод сделан по общему объёму заказов, частоте заказов и запасу сверх прогноза.

- **Сколько заказывать.** Заказать чуть больше прогноза выгодно. В среднем спрос примерно на 4,6 % выше прогноза. Каждая непроданная из-за нехватки единица стоит 10–13 (упущенная маржа 5 плюс неустойка 5 или 8). Лишняя единица обходится в 0,2–0,4 за день хранения, а если пропадёт, то в 7.
- **Как часто заказывать.** Ежедневный заказ платит фиксированные 19 примерно на 13 дней больше, чем заказ раз в два дня, то есть около 247. Зато средний запас меньше примерно на половину дневного спроса, это экономит около 300 на хранении. Поэтому ежедневные планы немного выгоднее, если запас сверх прогноза у них сравнимый.
- **Слабые кандидаты.**
  - Кандидаты 0, 2 и 6 заказывают ровно по прогнозу или около того, без запаса, поэтому получат больше неустоек.
  - Кандидат 1 по товару 0 покрывает только около 91 % ожидаемого спроса.
  - Кандидат 5 в первый день почти не заказывает сверх прогноза, чтобы покрыть начальную нехватку. В конце месяца он сильно режет заказы и рассчитывает на накопленный запас, а это рискованно.
- **Сильнейшие кандидаты.** Это 3, 4 и 7, у всех объём около 1,02–1,03 от ожидаемого спроса. Кандидат 7 заказывает раз в два дня, поэтому у него больше расходы на хранение.
- **Почему 3, а не 4.** Кандидат 3 сильнее закрывает начальную нехватку (53/52 против 42/41). Он держит запас сверх прогноза в середине месяца и уменьшает заказы к концу, чтобы меньше товара осталось в последний день. Остатки в конце ничего не стоят.

I picked **candidate 7**. I estimated the totals by hand under mean demand and didn't simulate any plan, so the ranking is approximate.

1. **Losses common to every plan.** At the start there are 50 units of item 0 against about 77 units of demand over days 0–1. There are 51 units of item 1 against about 86 over days 0–2. No order can arrive in time to cover these days, so every plan takes the same early shortage.
2. **Daily plans (0, 2, 3, 4, 5)** pay the 19 order fee about 28 times, roughly 530 in total.
   - Candidate 0 orders exactly the forecast. Actual demand averages about 4.6% above forecast, so stock runs down and shortages build up. Each missed unit costs 10 for item 0 and 13 for item 1.
   - Candidate 2 orders item 0 exactly at forecast, so it has the same problem on that item.
   - Candidate 5 orders about 15% above forecast and builds a buffer of about 80 units of each item. By day 25 it would hold about 109 units of item 0 and about 221 of item 1, roughly 330 in total. That exceeds the 268 capacity, so about 60 units of item 1 would be lost. It also pays more storage on that buffer.
